blocks.x: Over the past few decades, I'd argue that the Dutch oven has eclipsed the stand mixer as the most crucial piece of kitchen equipment for making a kitchen feel like a home kitchen. Is it because they're heavy and expensive? It it because couples always put them on their wedding registries? Is it because you can make soup in them and soup is comforting and feels homey and there's something to that? Not entirely sure. I can say though, that setting down one of these colorful, enameled hunks of cast iron onto a stove is akin to dropping an anchor. By committing to making a Sunday braise in a Dutch oven you're saying, “ This is my home, and because it's my home, I'm gonna make the entire place, and my clothes, smell like ragú.”

But which to buy? I've spent years and years thinking about this, because the question of what the best Dutch oven is, is a question that requires a lot of caveats and asterisks. Yes, there are certainly some design and quality metrics that help distinguish the Staubs and Le Creusets from Amazon Basics, but the bottom line is: Every Dutch oven on the market will deliver an extremely similar cooking performance. What it all comes down to is quality and design.

Cheap Dutch ovens work just fine, but their affordability comes at the cost of quality control. Budget Dutch ovens consistently feature manufacturer defects, chipping, and thinner enamel layers that can lead to accelerated wear and rusting.

As for design, while there are some practical advantages that some have over others, a lot of it comes down to subjective preferences. There are two people who have worked on this test over the years and we have vehemently disagreed with each other over the top spot, though, to be clear both of our choices are great Dutch ovens.

I'll get more into the two that always tussle for the top spot, as well as the most well-designed budget picks that also come with lifetime warranties. Keep reading to learn about how I and my team have tested Dutch ovens over the years, how to keep the enamel in tip-top shape, and which brands didn’t make the short list.
New in this update: I added reviews for the Crockpot, Goldilocks, and Müeller Dutch ovens, and moved Le Creuset into a clear top spot.

Interior enamel: Light and smooth
Available sizes: 2-qt., 4.5-qt., 5.5-qt., 7.25-qt., 9-qt., 13.75-qt.
Weight (5.5-qt. size): 11.6 lb.
Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer
Heat resistance: 500ºF
Warranty: Limited lifetime

What I love: We’ve been recommending Le Creuset’s Dutch ovens for as long as we’ve been recommending Dutch ovens. So if you have your heart set on one of these iconic pieces and you’re wondering whether it’s still a wise investment, the answer is a resounding yes.

Le Creuset’s smooth, sand-colored interior enamel produced a beautiful, even sear—and the light enamel makes it easy to keep an eye on browning and fond development. Le Creuset’s 5.5-quart Dutch oven also weighs about a pound less than Staub’s with thin loop handles that are easy to grip with or without oven mitts. The lighter weight comes courtesy of noticeably thinner cast iron, but it’s still thick enough to offer wonderful heat retention. Le Creuset Dutch ovens typically have a wider cooking surface and lower sides. This means more space for searing meats for braising—an essential Dutch oven task.

A few years ago Le Creuset began offering metal knobs on its Dutch ovens, which was a meaningful upgrade as the old phenolic knobs could melt if you tried to do something like use your Dutch oven to bake bread at 450℉, it would melt.

Then there is the manufacturing quality. Le Creuset is a century-old French brand, and though some of its cookware and tableware is now made in other countries, all of the enameled cast-iron cookware—including the Dutch ovens—is still made in the original manufacturing facility in Fresnoy-le-Grand, France. And while we know from experience with inherited pieces that the chip-resistant enamel can last a lifetime (with proper care, of course), Le Creuset Dutch ovens do come with a limited lifetime warranty.

What I’d leave: When covered at a boil, the Le Creuset may sputter at the edges a little. If you choose a Dutch oven with light-colored interior enamel, and cook in it often, you should expect some gradual discoloration. If you’re intent on keeping it pristine, you may jeopardize the lifespan of the enamel. Abrasive cleaners can wear the seal off of it and lead to even more staining.
